# Which measurements should the team confirm?

A clinic plans to recruit 500 unrelated people to study whether a DNA variant
is more common in patients with a disease than in unaffected controls. Everyone
will receive a routine diagnosis and a laboratory genotype call. The team can
pay for a specialist's diagnostic review and a confirmatory assay, but cannot
give both to everyone. A case recorded as a control can make the groups look
more alike. An incorrect genotype call can obscure a difference even when the
diagnosis is right. Can the team still detect the difference it expects? Which
measurements would be most useful to confirm, and how many people would it
need for 80% power?

The **Likelihood Ratio Test Allowing for Error (LRTae)** compares two
explanations for the measurements: the true genotype distribution is the same
in cases and controls, or it differs. Both explanations allow routine
measurements to be wrong. When a routine result and a more reliable result
are available for the same person, the pair helps distinguish a measurement
error from a real difference between groups.

Here **validation** means checking a person's measurement against a reference
assessment. It is different from testing the accuracy of statistical software.
In **double-sampling**, some people receive both the routine measurement and
the reference assessment of the same trait. Keep the routine result even
when the two disagree. The model treats the reference result as the truth;
a specialist review or second assay does not automatically meet that standard.

This is a *prospective* calculation: before anyone is recruited, we specify
what the study might look like and ask how often the test would detect the
assumed association. To run the examples, first load the package.

```{r load-package}
library(paweh)
```

# Decide who receives each reference assessment

The **phenotype** is the person's disease status. The **genotype** here is
the number of copies of one chosen allele (version of the DNA sequence).
Everyone gets both routine measurements. The four tiers in the diagram
describe only what is added. For example, someone who receives both reference
assessments belongs in the fourth tier and is counted once.

```{r tier-counts}
tier_counts <- list(
  n_fallible = 248,
  n_pheno_validated = 135,
  n_geno_validated = 72,
  n_both_validated = 45
)
```

```{r tier-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.7, fig.alt="All 500 receive routine diagnosis and genotyping. Of these, 248 have no reference assessment, 135 have diagnosis confirmed only, 72 have genotype confirmed only and 45 have both confirmed.", fig.cap="The two decisions cross: read down for diagnostic review and across for the confirmatory genotype assay. Each participant occupies one cell."}
op <- par(mar = rep(0.3, 4))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 6), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
text(5, 5.55, "All 500 receive routine diagnosis and genotyping", font = 2)
text(c(4, 8), 4.72, c("No confirmatory assay", "Confirm genotype"), font = 2)
text(0.1, c(3.35, 1.22), c("No diagnostic\nreview", "Review\ndiagnosis"), adj = 0)
x <- c(4, 4, 8, 8)
y <- c(3.35, 1.22, 3.35, 1.22)
rect(x - 1.85, y - 0.90, x + 1.85, y + 0.90,
     col = c("#F1F3F3", "#DCECEA", "#E0EBF6", "#D3E2DE"), border = "#526773")
text(x, y + 0.23, unlist(tier_counts), cex = 1.35, font = 2)
text(x, y - 0.36, c("Routine only", "Phenotype only", "Genotype only", "Both"))
par(op)
```

The four counts add to **500 individual participants**, including 180 with a
reference diagnosis (135 + 45) and 117 with a reference genotype (72 + 45).
The two reference-assessment totals overlap; adding them would count 45 people
twice. There are no family trios in this design.

For `lrtae_ncp()` and `lrtae_power()`, supply these four **counts** because
the study size is fixed. For `lrtae_mssn()`, the total is what we want to
find. Supply the same four categories as **shares** of whatever total will be
recruited: 49.6%, 27.0%, 14.4% and 9.0%, respectively.

# Describe the study before routine measurement

For a single variant with two alleles, let 0, 1 and 2 mean copies of the
chosen allele. For example, if that allele is A, the genotypes GG, AG and AA
have 0, 1 and 2 copies. Always use this order, and count the same allele, in
both groups and in the error matrix.

| Argument | What to supply |
|:---|:---|
| `true_control_genotype_frequencies` | Fractions of true controls with 0, 1 and 2 copies, before any measurement errors. |
| `true_case_genotype_frequencies` | The corresponding fractions *among true cases*. They describe the association the team wants to be able to detect. |
| `true_sampling_proportions` | The planned fractions of study participants who are true controls and true cases, in that order. |

Each vector sums to one (up to numerical rounding); its entries must be
positive. These supplied design values are deterministic: running the example
again uses the same numbers.

```{r historical-frequencies}
p_control <- c(0.5645454545, 0.3739393939, 0.0615151515)
p_case <- c(0.36, 0.48, 0.16)
q <- c(0.5, 0.5)
```

Here about 6.15% of true controls and 16% of true cases carry two copies.
That difference is part of the assumed association. In `q = c(0.5, 0.5)`,
half of the sample is expected to be true controls and half true cases.
Investigators can recruit equal groups even for a rare disease: `q` describes
the study composition, not disease prevalence in the source population. With
imperfect diagnoses the proportions *recorded* as cases and controls can also
differ from `q`.

## From true categories to routine results

For each true category, imagine following 100 people through the routine
measurement. Where would their results be recorded? The probabilities of
those destinations form one **row** of a misclassification matrix. Columns
are the **observed** categories. Diagonal entries mean the measurement is
correct. `byrow = TRUE` fills the R matrix one true category at a time.

```{r historical-errors}
phenotype_error <- matrix(
  c(0.98, 0.02,
    0.04, 0.96),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)
genotype_error <- matrix(
  c(0.965, 0.025, 0.010,
    0.025, 0.950, 0.025,
    0.010, 0.025, 0.965),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)
```

```{r matrix-labels, echo=FALSE}
show_matrix <- function(m, labels) {
  dimnames(m) <- list(paste("True", labels), paste("Observed", labels))
  knitr::kable(m, digits = 3)
}
show_matrix(phenotype_error, c("control", "case"))
```

Among **true controls**, 98% are recorded as controls and 2% as cases.
Among **true cases**, 4% are recorded as controls and 96% as cases. The
second row does *not* say that 4% of recorded controls have the disease:
that would ask the reverse question.

```{r genotype-labels, echo=FALSE}
show_matrix(genotype_error, 0:2)
```

Read the middle row from left to right. If the true genotype has **one
copy**, the routine assay calls zero copies 2.5% of the time, one copy 95%,
and two copies 2.5%. Each row accounts for all possible calls and sums to
one. Both matrices are assumptions for planning; `paweh` does not estimate
them from patient records. A team might use a pilot study with paired
assessments to choose plausible values.

**Where did these inputs come from?** The package examples and earlier draft
attribute them to a development workbook; an independent copy establishing
the complete input set was not verified. There is a close published relative.
Gordon, Finch and Kim (2020), section 4.2.1.4, pp. 138–141, give the same genotype
frequencies to printed precision and the same genotype error matrix. Their
500-person replicate has 45 people checked on both traits; Tables 4.1–4.2
give 117 genotype and 180 phenotype checks in total, consistent with all
four counts above. But the book uses 5% for a true case recorded as a
control, versus 4% here. Its fitted statistic of 24.1626 (p. 144) is for
one simulated dataset. The calculations below illustrate a design; they do
not reproduce that statistic or a published power benchmark.

# Will 500 people suffice, and how many are needed?

Collect the assumptions under the function argument names so that the same
inputs can be reused. In R, `do.call()` passes a list of named arguments to a
function. The fixed-design calls combine the model inputs with `tier_counts`.

```{r model-inputs}
model_inputs <- list(
  true_control_genotype_frequencies = p_control,
  true_case_genotype_frequencies = p_case,
  true_sampling_proportions = q,
  phenotype_misclassification_matrix = phenotype_error,
  genotype_misclassification_matrix = genotype_error
)
```

Start with `lrtae_ncp()`. Its **noncentrality parameter (NCP)** measures how
far the expected test-statistic distribution under the assumed association
separates from the distribution under no association. Equal true genotype
frequencies give zero separation. At the same significance level and degrees
of freedom, a larger NCP gives a greater chance of detecting the association.
The NCP describes a study design; it is neither an observed test statistic
nor a p-value.

```{r historical-ncp}
historical_ncp <- do.call(lrtae_ncp, c(model_inputs, tier_counts))
```

Use `lrtae_power()` to translate that separation into a probability.
`alpha = 0.05` sets a nominal 5% chance of declaring association when there
is none. The large-sample test has two degrees of freedom: once two of the
three genotype frequencies are known, the third must complete the sum to
one. Power is the chance of exceeding the test's cutoff *if the specified
case and control frequencies really differ as assumed*.

```{r historical-power}
historical_power <- do.call(
  lrtae_power,
  c(model_inputs, tier_counts, list(alpha = 0.05))
)
```

Now turn the question around. **Target power** of 0.80 means the team wants
to detect that difference in at least 80% of comparable studies. Ask
`lrtae_mssn()` for the minimum sample size necessary (MSSN). Keep the error
matrices, genotype frequencies, case/control mix and significance level the
same; replace fixed counts with the requested proportions.

```{r historical-mssn}
historical_mssn <- do.call(
  lrtae_mssn,
  c(
    model_inputs,
    list(
      target_power = 0.80,
      alpha = 0.05,
      prop_fallible = 248 / 500,
      prop_pheno_validated = 135 / 500,
      prop_geno_validated = 72 / 500,
      prop_both_validated = 45 / 500
    )
  )
)
```

```{r recruitment-summary, echo=FALSE}
fixed <- historical_power
needed <- historical_mssn
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Question = c("Recruit 500 as planned", "Recruit for 80% power"),
  Participants = c(fixed$N_total, needed$MSSN_total),
  NCP = round(c(historical_ncp, needed$achieved_ncp), 4),
  Power = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * c(fixed$power, needed$achieved_power))
))
```

**The 500-person plan exceeds the target.** Its NCP of 22.4083 corresponds
to 99.25% power: about 99 in 100 studies would detect this particular
difference if the assumptions hold. At the same validation shares, the team
can meet its 80% target with **216 participants**. Their integer allocation
gives 80.22% power. Neither percentage is the probability that the variant
causes the disease.

## Turn validation shares into people

A clinic cannot book a fraction of a participant. The **Hamilton
largest-remainder rule** first gives each tier the whole part of its quota.
It then gives the remaining places, one each, to the tiers with the largest
fractional remainders. The package resolves exact ties in its argument
order: routine only, phenotype only, genotype only, then both.

Try it with just **10 places** and the same shares. The quotas are
4.96, 2.70, 1.44 and 0.90. Start with 4, 2, 1 and 0 people. The three
remaining places go to routine only (0.96), both (0.90) and phenotype only
(0.70), giving **5 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 10**. This illustrates rounding, not
a recommendation to run a ten-person study.

Apply the same rule to the 216-person recruitment plan:

```{r allocation-rounding, echo=FALSE}
tier_names <- c("Routine only", "Phenotype only", "Genotype only", "Both")
shares <- unlist(tier_counts) / fixed$N_total
quota <- needed$MSSN_total * shares
assigned <- unname(unlist(needed[names(tier_counts)]))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Tier = tier_names, Share = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * shares),
  Quota = sprintf("%.3f", quota), Whole = floor(quota),
  Remainder = sprintf("%.3f", quota - floor(quota)), Assigned = assigned,
  row.names = NULL
))
```

The whole parts sum to 215. The largest remainder is 0.440 in the
both-validated tier, so its 19 becomes 20. The final counts are
**107 + 58 + 31 + 20 = 216**. The last tier now has 20/216, or about 9.26%,
slightly above the requested 9%. The rule keeps the counts close to the
requested shares while filling every place. It does not search for the best
use of a validation budget.

# Which checks make a difference at 220 people?

Suppose recruitment is capped at 220. The team can change the reference
assessments but keeps the same biological assumptions, measurement errors,
case/control mix and 5% significance level. Each row below is a different
plan for those same 220 places. In particular, the two focused designs move
33 checks from one measurement to the other without changing the number
of people checked.

```{r validation-comparison}
allocations <- data.frame(
  design = c(
    "Low validation", "Phenotype focused", "Genotype focused", "Balanced"
  ),
  n_fallible = c(198, 154, 154, 110),
  n_pheno_validated = c(9, 44, 11, 33),
  n_geno_validated = c(9, 11, 44, 33),
  n_both_validated = c(4, 11, 11, 44),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

design_results <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(allocations)), function(index) {
  counts <- as.list(allocations[index, 2:5])
  do.call(lrtae_power, c(model_inputs, counts, list(alpha = 0.05)))
})
allocations$N_total <- rowSums(allocations[2:5])
allocations$NCP <- vapply(design_results, function(x) x$ncp, numeric(1))
allocations$Power <- vapply(design_results, function(x) x$power, numeric(1))
```

```{r comparison-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  transform(allocations, NCP = round(NCP, 4), Power = sprintf("%.3f%%", 100 * Power)),
  col.names = c("Design", "Routine only", "Phenotype only", "Genotype only",
                "Both", "Total", "NCP", "Power")
)
```

```{r validation-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Four horizontal power bars. Only the balanced design crosses the dashed line at 80 percent.", fig.cap="Probability of detecting the assumed association at 220 people. The dashed line marks the 80% target."}
old_par <- par(mar = c(4.3, 10.0, 1.0, 1.0))
barplot(
  allocations$Power,
  names.arg = allocations$design,
  horiz = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Prospective power",
  las = 1,
  col = "#355C7D",
  border = NA
)
abline(v = 0.80, lty = 2, col = "#7A4F5B")
par(old_par)
```

Only the balanced design clears 80% (81.63%). It puts 110 people in at
least one validation tier, including 44 who get both checks. The
low-validation plan checks just 22 people and reaches 78.17%. The focused
plans reach 79.568% and 79.576%: switching the focus has little practical
effect here, and neither reaches the target. This comparison holds
recruitment fixed, **not spending**. Confirming both measurements for more
people may cost substantially more. Different error rates, genotype
frequencies or validation costs could favor a different plan.

# Technical detail: what information does validation add?

The contrast of interest, \(\Delta\), is the difference between control and
case frequencies for the first two genotypes. The third difference is
determined by the first two. The direction here is control minus case.
The expected information measures how precisely the planned measurements
can distinguish these differences. A reference diagnosis tells us which
disease group a participant actually belongs to; a reference genotype tells
us which genotype category contributed the observation. The four tiers
therefore contribute different amounts of information per person.

The NCP combines the size of the assumed difference with the information
available to detect it:

\[
\lambda = \Delta^{\mathsf T} I_{\mathrm{eff}} \Delta .
\]

Why *efficient* information? The association contrasts are not the only
unknowns in an eventual analysis. The background genotype distribution
and the true sampling mix also affect what is observed. Those are
**nuisance parameters** for this question: necessary to describe the data,
but not the differences being tested. The calculation allows for uncertainty
about them even though planning values are supplied.

## The information matrix and its Schur complement

The package adds the expected information from each tier, weighted by its
participant count. Write the resulting matrix in blocks for the frequency
contrasts \(\psi\) and nuisance parameters \(\eta\). Here \(\eta\) consists
of the free case genotype frequencies and the true control sampling share.
The error-matrix entries are held fixed in this calculation. The **Schur
complement** is the block calculation

\[
I_{\mathrm{eff}} =
 I_{\psi\psi} - I_{\psi\eta} I_{\eta\eta}^{-1} I_{\eta\psi}.
\]

The first term is the information about the contrasts if the nuisance
parameters were known. The subtraction accounts for information shared
with those parameters. With three genotype categories, the 5% cutoff of
the central chi-square distribution on two degrees of freedom is about
5.9915. Power is the area above that same cutoff in a noncentral chi-square
distribution with the design's NCP. This uses expected measurements across
possible studies; no likelihood is fitted to an individual dataset.

# What could make the plan unreliable?

**Can the measurements distinguish the explanations?** If many people have
a positive routine diagnosis, that could reflect more true cases or more
false positives. Without enough paired routine and reference diagnoses,
the observed labels alone may not identify both explanations separately.
This is an **identifiability** problem. In an analysis that estimates error
rates, the corresponding validation data help separate them. Here the rates
are supplied; too little independent information about the modeled frequency
parameters can still make the nuisance information matrix singular (it has
no inverse). A singularity means this calculation cannot distinguish the
required parameters for that design. It does not mean that every tier must
be nonempty or that every method for misclassification will fail.

**Would the assumptions travel to this clinic?** The calculation uses one
phenotype error matrix across genotypes and one genotype error matrix across
disease groups; the model combines these error processes independently given
the true categories. If the confirmatory assessment itself often errs,
the pilot differs from the recruits, or the laboratory calls cases less
accurately than controls, the quoted power may be misleading. Before choosing
a recruitment target, rerun the design with plausible higher and lower error
rates (adjust each diagonal so its row still sums to one) and with a smaller
case/control difference. The power calculation uses a large-sample
approximation, which also warrants caution with sparse categories.

**Do you have a design or patient records?** These functions take design
probabilities and tier sizes. Barral et al. describe software that instead
fits likelihoods to observed counts and tests an association. That requires
observed data and estimation steps outside the scope of these planning
functions. LTTae is a different, trend-based test that assigns scores to
genotypes; LRTae here tests differences in the genotype distribution.
Neither sequencing depth nor individual read errors are inputs. For a study
starting from sequence reads, see the
[sequencing study design vignette](paweh-06-sequencing-study-design.html).

# Methods and references

- Ji F, Yang Y, Haynes C, Finch SJ, Gordon D. [Computing asymptotic power and
  sample size for case-control genetic association studies in the presence of
  phenotype and/or genotype misclassification errors](https://doi.org/10.2202/1544-6115.1184).
  *Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology*. 2005;4:Article 37.
  This is the primary methodological source for the prospective NCP and
  its use for power and recruitment. Integer tier assignment is described
  here as a package rule.
- Barral S, Haynes C, Stone M, Gordon D. [LRTae: improving statistical power
  for genetic association with case/control data when phenotype and/or genotype
  misclassification errors are present](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2156-7-24).
  *BMC Genetics*. 2006;7:24. This paper describes the observed-data software
  and illustrates its use with an ankylosing spondylitis application.
- Gordon D, Finch SJ, Kim W. [*Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics: How to
  Assess, Address, and Account for Mixtures in Association Studies*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-61121-7).
  Springer; 2020. Chapter 4, sections 4.2.1.1–4.2.1.4, covers the measurement
  groups, observed likelihoods, test and worked example; section 4.2.2
  introduces LTTae. Chapter 5, section 5.2.3, discusses *empirical* LRTae
  power from simulations, a different route from the analytical power above.
